title: Why the Cabin Lights Dim When Your Plane Lands
fb_caption: Right before landing, the cabin lights go down, and it isn't to help you nap. Your eyes need minutes to adjust to the dark, so dimming early gives them a head start. If everyone ever had to leave in a hurry, the floor lights and exit signs would already stand out. Many airlines also ask for window shades up so the crew can see outside and choose a safe exit. And to be certified, big airliners must show everyone can get out in 90 seconds, in the dark, using only half the exits. Window seat or aisle seat: which do you pick?
engagement_comment: Window seat or aisle seat: which do you pick? 1 = window, always, 2 = aisle, always, 3 = whatever's open.
sources: AFAR, Why Do Airplanes Dim the Cabin Lights During Takeoff and Landing? (eyes adjust in advance for an evacuation; exit and floor path lights easier to see; shades and dimming work together): https://www.afar.com/magazine/why-airplanes-dim-cabin-lights-for-takeoff-and-landing

Mental Floss, Why Planes Dim Lights During Takeoff and Landing (dark adaptation before a possible evacuation; seeing outside): https://mentalfloss.com/transportation/planes-and-airports/why-planes-dim-lights-during-takeoff-and-landing

AFAR, Why Do Window Shades Have to Be Open for Takeoff and Landing? (FAA does not regulate shade position; airline policy; crew can see hazards outside; IATA/EASA guidance): https://www.afar.com/magazine/why-do-window-shades-have-to-be-open-for-takeoff-and-landing
14 CFR 25.803 (airplanes with more than 44 passenger seats: everyone evacuated to the ground within 90 seconds under simulated emergency conditions): https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/25.803
14 CFR Appendix J to Part 25 (demonstration in darkness, only emergency lighting; exits used = one exit from each exit pair, i.e. half): https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/appendix-J_to_part_25

beats.text: Your plane is about to land, and the cabin lights go dim. That's on purpose.
Your eyes need minutes to adjust to the dark. Dimming early gives them a head start.
So if you ever had to leave in a hurry, the floor lights and exit signs would already stand out.
Many airlines also ask for window shades up, so the crew can see outside and choose a safe exit.
Here's the twist. To be certified, big airliners must show everyone can get out in ninety seconds, in the dark, using only half the exits.
Window seat or aisle seat: which do you pick? Tell us below.
